opus-5.5.text:
I think NVIDIA's role is really to be an enabler for the whole ecosystem. We see world models as one of the most important frontiers in AI right now, especially for physical AI — robotics, autonomous vehicles, anything that needs to understand and act in the real three-dimensional world. And it's a very hard problem. No single company is going to solve it alone.

So when we look at teams like Fei-Fei's World Labs or Yann's new effort, we're genuinely excited. These are people with deep scientific vision, and they're approaching the problem from different angles. Fei-Fei has long emphasized spatial intelligence — understanding 3D structure, geometry, how the world is laid out. Yann has been very vocal about learning predictive representations, models that capture how the world evolves without necessarily generating every pixel. Those are complementary perspectives, and the field benefits from having multiple bets.

From our side, we support them in a few ways. The most obvious is compute — training world models is extremely expensive, because you're dealing with video, 3D, long horizons, multimodal data. Beyond hardware, we try to provide the software stack and the platforms that lower the barrier. With Cosmos, for example, we released open world foundation models, tokenizers, and data curation pipelines, so that researchers and startups don't have to rebuild everything from scratch. The idea is: if we open up good base models and tools, others can post-train, specialize, and push in their own directions.

My personal view is that NVIDIA does well when the whole field moves forward. We're not trying to be the only world-model company. We want to build foundational pieces, share them openly where we can, and help partners — whether a big lab, a startup, or an academic group — go faster. If World Labs or AMI makes a breakthrough, that's good for physical AI overall, and I think good for us too.

And honestly, as a researcher, it's just fun to have strong people working on this. Competition and collaboration both push the science forward, and world models are still early. There's a lot we don't know yet — what the right representation is, how to evaluate them, how to make them truly useful for decision-making. Having many groups attacking it from different sides is how we'll find out.

r001.rationale: The response describes World Labs’ focus on spatial intelligence and AMI’s focus on predictive representations as complementary approaches, and says NVIDIA supports multiple bets.

r002.rationale: It presents Cosmos models and tools as lowering barriers for researchers and startups, but does not identify them specifically as a resource for companies with less funding than World Labs or AMI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, I think it's wonderful that people like Fei-Fei and Yann are working on world models. They are pioneers, and the fact that they have started companies focused on this problem tells you how important the problem is. At NVIDIA, we don't see them as competitors in the traditional sense. The way I think about it, we are a platform company. Our job is to make the whole ecosystem succeed.

So concretely, there are a few layers where we support them. The most obvious one is compute. Training a world model is extremely expensive. You are dealing with video, with 3D, with physics, with very long sequences of tokens. The data volume is orders of magnitude larger than text. So they need GPUs, they need networking, they need the full stack, and we try to make that as efficient as possible for everyone.

The second layer is software and open models. With Cosmos, we released world foundation models openly, along with the tokenizers, the data curation pipeline, the guardrails. The intention is not to say "use our model instead of yours." The intention is to give everyone a starting point so that nobody has to reinvent the basics. If World Labs or AMI wants to take some component, fine-tune it, or build something completely different on top, that's a success for us. The more people who build world models, the more compute the world needs, and frankly the faster the whole field moves toward physical AI.

The third layer is the application side, which I think people sometimes underestimate. Robotics companies, autonomous vehicle companies, simulation companies all run on our platforms, Omniverse, Isaac, DRIVE. Those are the eventual customers of world models. So when a world model company has a great model, we want it to plug naturally into those pipelines. We are kind of the connective tissue between the model builders and the people who actually deploy robots in a factory or cars on the road.

And honestly, from a research point of view, I'm very happy to see different bets. Yann's approach with JEPA, predicting in latent space rather than pixels, is philosophically a bit different from how we started with Cosmos, which is more generative. Fei-Fei's team is very focused on spatial intelligence and 3D. Nobody knows yet which direction will win, or whether they will converge. Having multiple serious teams exploring in parallel is healthy. Our role is to make sure that whichever path works out, the infrastructure is there to scale it.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes JEPA’s latent-space approach, Cosmos’s generative approach, and Fei-Fei’s focus on spatial intelligence, and says NVIDIA provides infrastructure to scale whichever approach works.

r002.rationale: The response describes Cosmos as an open starting point that helps builders avoid reinventing basics, but does not connect it to companies with less funding than World Labs or AMI.

astra-6.text:
I think NVIDIA’s role is to enable a broad ecosystem. World models are a very ambitious direction, and different teams will take different approaches to how these models learn, represent the world, and make predictions. We want to provide the computing platform and software tools that help researchers explore those ideas and turn them into useful systems.

I can’t speak to specific arrangements with World Labs or AMI, but the opportunity is broader than any one company. If we can make it easier to train models, simulate environments, and evaluate their behavior, we can help the whole field move forward. There’s still a lot to discover, so supporting that diversity of approaches is valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says different teams will take different approaches to learning, representing, and predicting, and describes NVIDIA as providing tools and computing to support that ecosystem.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Cosmos or identify it as a resource for less-funded companies.

sol-6.1.text:
I see NVIDIA’s role as enabling a broad ecosystem. World models are an exciting research direction, but there are still many open questions about representations, architectures, and how to evaluate what these models actually understand. Different teams will pursue different approaches, and that diversity is valuable.

For companies like the ones you mentioned, NVIDIA can help through computing infrastructure, software, and research collaboration. The goal is to make it easier for teams to test ideas and scale what works. I wouldn’t speak for their specific plans or imply any particular partnership, but broadly, we want researchers and companies to have the tools to push this field forward.

r001.rationale: The response says different teams will pursue different approaches and that this diversity is valuable, framing NVIDIA’s support as enabling that range of approaches.

r002.rationale: Cosmos is not mentioned, nor does the response identify a resource aimed at companies with less funding than World Labs or AMI.
